mcqs.q: Based on pathophysiology, how many forms of periodontitis does the 2017 classification recognise?
mcqs.explain: Necrotizing periodontitis, periodontitis as a direct manifestation of systemic diseases, and periodontitis.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three forms of periodontitis?
opts: Periodontitis as a direct manifestation of systemic diseases
mcqs.explain: The chronic/aggressive split was abandoned; the third form is simply periodontitis, described by stage and grade.

mcqs.q: The pseudomembrane covering the ulcerated gingiva in necrotizing periodontal disease is described as:
mcqs.explain: A yellowish-white or grayish slough or pseudomembrane covers the necrotic papillary and marginal gingiva.

mcqs.q: Which shape change of the papillae characterises necrotizing periodontal disease?
mcqs.explain: Blunting and cratering of the papillae is one of the defining clinical features.

mcqs.q: Besides pain and bleeding, which oral symptom is typical of necrotizing periodontal disease?
opts: Loss of taste for sweet foods
Burning of the dorsum of the tongue
Persistent salty discharge from the palate
mcqs.explain: Fetid breath accompanies the bleeding and pain; fever, malaise and lymphadenopathy may also occur.

mcqs.q: Necrotizing periodontitis differs from necrotizing gingivitis by the presence of:
opts: A grayish pseudomembrane over the papillae
mcqs.explain: Clinical features are otherwise similar; NP adds attachment and bone loss.

mcqs.q: Necrotizing periodontitis is often observed in:
opts: HIV-positive individuals with low CD4 counts
Patients with a long-standing fixed prosthesis
mcqs.explain: Advanced immunosuppression with a low CD4 count is the classical association.

mcqs.q: Necrotizing stomatitis is distinguished from the other necrotizing diseases by:
opts: Soft tissue necrosis extending beyond the gingiva with bone denudation
Necrosis confined to the interdental papillae only
An absence of pain despite extensive necrosis
The absence of any microbial component
mcqs.explain: NS is the most severe form, with bone denudation and bony sequestrum or osteitis.

mcqs.q: Which group of predisposing factors is listed for necrotizing periodontal diseases?
opts: Psychological stress, smoking, immunosuppression and malnutrition
Crowding, overhangs, calculus and oral dryness
mcqs.explain: All four lower host resistance rather than increase the bacterial load.

mcqs.q: Necrotizing periodontal diseases respond well to:
opts: Antimicrobial therapy combined with professional plaque and calculus removal
Surgical excision of the necrotic tissue alone
mcqs.explain: They are microbial, infectious conditions, so antimicrobials plus mechanical debridement are effective.

mcqs.q: In periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease, the major effect on the periodontium is through:
opts: Direct bacterial invasion of the alveolar bone
Reduced salivary flow and buffering capacity
mcqs.explain: Hematologic and genetic disorders act by altering host immunity.

mcqs.q: A characteristic clinical pattern of periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease is:
opts: Onset at an early age with rapid attachment loss and early tooth loss
Onset after the fifth decade with slow, steady bone loss
Localisation to the maxillary anterior sextant only
A complete absence of bleeding on probing
mcqs.explain: Early age of onset with rapid CAL and early tooth loss is typical.

mcqs.q: In periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease, removal of local factors is:
opts: Inadequate to arrest the periodontal destruction
Sufficient to arrest the destruction in most cases
Contraindicated until the systemic disease resolves
The only treatment needed once the disease is diagnosed
mcqs.explain: The underlying disease is the major predisposing factor, so debridement alone will not stop the destruction.

mcqs.q: Which triad of criteria diagnoses Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome?
opts: Palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, loss of both dentitions, autosomal-recessive inheritance
Palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, delayed eruption, autosomal-dominant inheritance
Gingival fibromatosis, loss of both dentitions, X-linked inheritance
mcqs.explain: These three criteria together establish the diagnosis of PLS.

mcqs.q: The gene mutated in Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome is:
mcqs.explain: A mutation in the cathepsin C gene underlies the autosomal-recessive condition.

mcqs.q: The primary cause of the periodontal destruction in Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome is:
opts: Deficient collagen cross-linking in the ligament
Defective enamel maturation at the cervical margin
Exaggerated osteoclast activity driven by parathyroid hormone
mcqs.explain: Neutrophil dysfunction leaves the host unable to control opportunistic periodontal pathogens.

mcqs.q: Signs of palmoplantar keratoderma in PLS usually appear:
opts: With the eruption of the first primary teeth at 5 to 6 months
Only after the permanent dentition is complete
In the second decade of life
At the time of the first permanent molar eruption
mcqs.explain: They usually appear simultaneously with the first primary teeth, but may appear as early as one month of age.

mcqs.q: Which finding is common in the family history of a PLS patient?
opts: A dominant transmission through every generation
mcqs.explain: Consanguinity is a common finding in this autosomal-recessive condition.

mcqs.q: Serum IgG titers in patients with Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome are typically elevated against:
mcqs.explain: Elevated anti-Aa IgG is the characteristic serological finding.

mcqs.q: The clinical feature that distinguishes periodontitis from gingivitis is:
opts: The presence of a dental biofilm
mcqs.explain: Attachment loss — as pocketing and/or recession — is the defining difference.

mcqs.q: Clinical attachment loss manifests clinically as:
opts: Periodontal pocket formation and/or recession of the marginal gingiva
Pocket formation only, since recession masks attachment loss
Recession only, since pockets reflect gingival swelling
Tooth mobility, which precedes any change in probing depth
mcqs.explain: Both pocketing and recession represent attachment loss, and either may be present.

mcqs.q: A patient is a periodontitis case when interdental CAL is detectable at:
opts: Any single tooth with a pocket over 5 mm
Thirty per cent or more of the teeth present
mcqs.explain: Interdental CAL at ≥2 non-adjacent teeth is the first case definition.

mcqs.q: The second case definition of periodontitis requires buccal or oral CAL of:
opts: ≥ 3 mm with pocketing > 3 mm at ≥ 2 teeth
≥ 3 mm with pocketing > 5 mm at ≥ 2 teeth
≥ 5 mm with pocketing > 3 mm at any one tooth
≥ 2 mm with pocketing > 4 mm at ≥ 3 teeth
mcqs.explain: Buccal or oral CAL ≥3 mm with pocketing >3 mm at ≥2 teeth, once non-periodontal causes are excluded.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-periodontal cause of attachment loss that must be excluded?
opts: An endodontic lesion draining through the sulcus
A deep interproximal pocket with bleeding on probing
Horizontal bone loss of the coronal third
Furcation involvement of a lower first molar
mcqs.explain: Draining endodontic lesions, traumatic recession, subgingival caries, distal CAL on second molars and vertical root fracture are the five exclusions.

mcqs.q: Attachment loss on the distal aspect of a second molar must be interpreted cautiously because it may be caused by:
opts: The adjacent third molar rather than periodontitis
Normal anatomical thinning of the distal bone plate
Occlusal trauma from a working-side interference
Routine probing error in the posterior sextant
mcqs.explain: It is one of the listed non-periodontal causes of observed CAL.

mcqs.q: Staging of periodontitis incorporates:
opts: Rate of progression and risk factors
mcqs.explain: Severity plus complexity defines the stage; progression rate and risk factors define the grade.

mcqs.q: The staging system determines severity from:
opts: The sites with the maximum attachment loss or bone loss
The mean attachment loss across all probed sites
The site with the deepest probing depth only
The total number of bleeding sites in the mouth
mcqs.explain: Staging highlights the patient's most severe areas of destruction.

mcqs.q: When counting tooth loss for staging, which teeth are included?
opts: Missing teeth and teeth identified for extraction due to periodontitis
Missing teeth only, whatever the cause of loss
Only teeth already extracted because of periodontitis
Only third molars lost for any reason
mcqs.explain: Teeth planned for extraction as part of active therapy count as well.

mcqs.q: If a deep probing depth is eliminated by treatment, the stage generally:
opts: Should not retrogress to a lower level
Must be recalculated and lowered at the next review
Is replaced by a grade instead of a stage
Becomes unclassifiable until five years have passed
mcqs.explain: Existing severity and previous complexity factors still predict future progression.

mcqs.q: The one exception that allows a stage to be retrograded is:
opts: Significant bone gain after successful regenerative therapy
Complete resolution of bleeding on probing
Cessation of smoking for more than five years
mcqs.explain: Only true bone gain after regeneration can move the stage down.

mcqs.q: Interdental CAL at the site of greatest loss in Stage I periodontitis is:
mcqs.explain: Stage I is 1–2 mm, Stage II is 3–4 mm, and Stages III and IV are ≥5 mm.

mcqs.q: Radiographic bone loss in Stage II periodontitis is:
opts: Extending to the mid-third of the root
mcqs.explain: Stage I is <15% and Stage II is 15–33%, both within the coronal third.

mcqs.q: Tooth loss due to periodontitis in Stage III is:
mcqs.explain: Stage III allows ≤4 teeth lost; ≥5 moves the case to Stage IV.

mcqs.q: Stage IV periodontitis is separated from Stage III mainly by:
opts: Tooth loss of five or more teeth and the need for complex rehabilitation
A greater interdental clinical attachment loss at the worst site
Deeper radiographic bone loss on the mid-third of the root
A higher percentage of teeth involved
mcqs.explain: Both have CAL ≥5 mm and mid-third bone loss; tooth loss and rehabilitation needs divide them.

mcqs.q: Maximum probing depth in the local complexity criteria for Stage II is:
mcqs.explain: Stage I is ≤4 mm, Stage II is ≤5 mm, and Stage III adds depths ≥6 mm.

mcqs.q: Which complexity factor first appears at Stage III?
opts: Furcation involvement Class II or III
Bite collapse with drifting and flaring
mcqs.explain: Stage III adds depths ≥6 mm, vertical bone loss ≥3 mm, Class II/III furcations and a moderate ridge defect.

mcqs.q: Vertical bone loss becomes a complexity criterion at Stage III when it reaches:
mcqs.explain: Vertical bone loss ≥3 mm is listed with the Stage III local complexity factors.

mcqs.q: Secondary occlusal trauma appears in the Stage IV complexity criteria at a tooth mobility of:
mcqs.explain: Mobility degree ≥2 is the threshold quoted for secondary occlusal trauma in Stage IV.

mcqs.q: The number of remaining teeth that signals the need for complex rehabilitation in Stage IV is:
opts: Fewer than 20 teeth, that is fewer than 10 opposing pairs
Fewer than 24 teeth, that is fewer than 12 opposing pairs
Fewer than 16 teeth, that is fewer than 8 opposing pairs
Fewer than 28 teeth, that is fewer than 14 opposing pairs
mcqs.explain: Less than 20 remaining teeth (10 opposing pairs) is the Stage IV criterion.

mcqs.q: Localized periodontitis is defined as involvement of:
opts: Fewer than four teeth in total
mcqs.explain: Localized is <30% and generalized is ≥30% of teeth at the stage-defining severity level.

mcqs.q: Besides localized and generalized, the third extent descriptor is:
mcqs.explain: Molar-incisor pattern is the third recognised distribution.

mcqs.q: Grading of periodontitis is principally an analysis of:
opts: The rate of disease progression and risk of further progression
The number of teeth lost and the complexity of rehabilitation
The percentage of teeth involved by the disease
The depth of the deepest pocket in the mouth
mcqs.explain: Grade covers progression rate, risk of further progression, risk factors and general health modifiers.

mcqs.q: Direct evidence of progression for grading comes from:
opts: The percentage of bone loss divided by the patient's age
The case phenotype relative to biofilm deposits
mcqs.explain: Longitudinal radiographic bone loss or CAL data is direct evidence; % bone loss/age is indirect.

mcqs.q: Grade B corresponds to direct evidence of bone loss or CAL of:
mcqs.explain: Grade A is no loss, grade B is <2 mm and grade C is ≥2 mm over 5 years.

mcqs.q: A percentage bone loss divided by age of 0.6 corresponds to:
opts: No grade can be assigned from this value
mcqs.explain: Grade A is <0.25, grade B is 0.25–1.0 and grade C is >1.0.

mcqs.q: Heavy biofilm deposits with low levels of destruction is the case phenotype of:
opts: A case that cannot be graded
mcqs.explain: Grade B is destruction commensurate with deposits, and grade C is destruction exceeding expectation.

mcqs.q: A molar-incisor pattern with a lack of expected response to standard bacterial control therapy indicates:
mcqs.explain: These are the specific clinical patterns listed for the grade C case phenotype.

mcqs.q: A patient smoking 14 cigarettes a day is assigned which grade modifier?
mcqs.explain: Non-smoker is A, fewer than 10 a day is B, and 10 or more a day is C.

mcqs.q: A diabetic patient with HbA1c of 6.4% is assigned which grade modifier?
opts: Grade A, because the HbA1c is below 7.0%
mcqs.explain: Grade A requires normoglycemia or no diagnosis of diabetes; a diabetic below 7.0% is grade B.

mcqs.q: Systemic diseases affecting the periodontal supporting structures act:
opts: Only by increasing the mass of the subgingival biofilm
Only in the presence of calculus
Through a direct toxic effect of plaque metabolites
mcqs.explain: They have a negative impact on the attachment apparatus independent of biofilm-induced inflammation.

mcqs.q: Which is listed as a neoplasm affecting the periodontal supporting tissues?
mcqs.explain: The neoplasm group is squamous cell carcinoma, odontogenic tumors, other primary and secondary metastatic neoplasms.

mcqs.q: Which disorder is listed under 'other disorders that may affect the periodontal tissues'?
mcqs.explain: The group holds Langerhans cell histiocytosis, giant cell granulomas, hyperparathyroidism and systemic sclerosis.

mcqs.q: A periodontal abscess is defined as a localized acute purulent infection within:
opts: The gingival wall of the periodontal pocket
The periapical tissues of a necrotic tooth
The follicular space of an impacted tooth
The marrow spaces of the alveolar bone
mcqs.explain: Its location in the pocket wall is what makes it periodontal rather than periapical.

mcqs.q: Periodontal abscesses are classified according to:
opts: The depth of the associated pocket
mcqs.explain: Pre-existing deep pockets, foreign body reactions and overgrowth of opportunistic bacteria are the aetiological groups.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT an aetiological category of periodontal abscess?
opts: Occlusal interference from a high restoration
mcqs.explain: Only the three listed categories are used.

mcqs.q: An endodontic–periodontal lesion is best defined as:
opts: A pathological communication between the pulpal and periodontal tissues
A periapical radiolucency without any pocket
A periodontal pocket adjacent to a vital tooth
A vertical bone defect caused by occlusal trauma
mcqs.explain: The defining feature is the pathological communication between the two tissue compartments.

mcqs.q: Which is listed as a trauma or iatrogenic cause of an endodontic–periodontal lesion?
opts: Furcation involvement from horizontal bone loss
mcqs.explain: Root fracture or cracking, root perforation, external root resorption and pulp necrosis are the listed causes.

mcqs.q: Which sign is characteristic of an endodontic–periodontal lesion?
opts: A deep periodontal pocket reaching the root apex
Generalized bleeding on probing with shallow pockets
Diffuse gingival enlargement covering the crowns
mcqs.explain: Pockets reaching the apex, with an altered response to pulp vitality testing, are the key findings.

mcqs.q: Gingival/soft tissue recession is subclassified in the mucogingival list into:
opts: Facial or lingual surfaces, and interproximal (papillary)
mcqs.explain: The two sub-headings follow the surface involved.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is listed under 'gingival excess'?
mcqs.explain: Gingival excess covers pseudo-pocket, inconsistent gingival margin, excessive gingival display and gingival enlargement.

mcqs.q: Gingival recession is defined as:
opts: An apical shift in the position of the gingival margin with root exposure
A coronal shift of the gingival margin over the crown
An increase in probing depth without attachment loss
Loss of the keratinized band without change in margin position
mcqs.explain: Apical migration of the margin exposing the root surface is the definition.

mcqs.q: The Cairo classification of gingival recession is based on:
opts: The width of the keratinized gingiva
The depth of the recession in millimetres
The thickness of the gingival biotype
mcqs.explain: Cairo compares interproximal with buccal attachment loss.

mcqs.q: Recession Type 1 (RT1) is characterised by:
opts: Buccal attachment loss with no interproximal attachment loss
Interproximal loss equal to the buccal loss
Interproximal loss greater than the buccal loss
Interproximal loss with no buccal loss
mcqs.explain: RT1 has an intact interproximal attachment level.

mcqs.q: Recession Type 3 (RT3) is characterised by interproximal attachment loss that is:
opts: Higher than the buccal attachment loss
Less than the buccal attachment loss
Equal to the buccal attachment loss
mcqs.explain: RT2 is interproximal ≤ buccal; RT3 is interproximal > buccal.

mcqs.q: A traumatic occlusal force is defined as an occlusal force that:
opts: Exceeds the reparative capacity of the periodontal attachment apparatus
Exceeds the yield strength of the enamel at the occlusal contact
Occurs outside the normal envelope of mandibular motion
Is generated during parafunction rather than during chewing
mcqs.explain: Exceeding the reparative capacity of the attachment apparatus is what results in occlusal trauma.

mcqs.q: The diagnosis of occlusal trauma is assisted by:
opts: Pulp vitality testing of the affected teeth
mcqs.explain: No single indicator is diagnostic; several clinical and radiographic findings are combined.

mcqs.q: Which is a localized TOOTH-related factor predisposing to gingival disease?
opts: Cervical enamel projections and enamel pearls
mcqs.explain: The tooth-related group holds enamel projections and pearls, developmental grooves, fractures and root resorption.

mcqs.q: Which is a localized PROSTHESIS-related factor predisposing to gingival disease?
mcqs.explain: Fixed restorations and prostheses, dental materials and removable prostheses form the prosthesis group.

mcqs.q: How many categories of peri-implant diseases and conditions does the classification list?
mcqs.explain: Peri-implant health, peri-implant mucositis, peri-implantitis, and soft and hard tissue deficiencies.

mcqs.q: Peri-implant health is defined by:
opts: Absence of visual signs of inflammation and lack of bleeding on probing
Absence of bone loss, whatever the soft tissue appearance
Probing depths of 3 mm or less around the implant
Absence of any plaque on the implant surface
mcqs.explain: No visual inflammation and no BOP defines peri-implant health.

mcqs.q: Peri-implant mucositis differs from peri-implantitis in that mucositis:
opts: Shows inflammation and/or BOP without loss of supportive or marginal bone
Shows bone loss without any visual inflammation
Shows neither inflammation nor bleeding on probing
Always follows an episode of peri-implantitis
mcqs.explain: The presence or absence of bone loss is what separates the two.

mcqs.q: Peri-implantitis is defined by inflammation and/or BOP accompanied by:
opts: Loss of the keratinized mucosa around the implant
mcqs.explain: Progressive loss of supporting bone is the defining feature.

saqs.q: Name the three forms of periodontitis recognised by the 2017 classification on the basis of pathophysiology.
saqs.a: Necrotizing periodontitis; periodontitis as a direct manifestation of systemic diseases; and periodontitis, which is then described by stage and grade.

list: (A) Necrotizing periodontitis
(B) Periodontitis as a direct manifestation of systemic diseases
(C) Periodontitis — described by stage and grade, replacing the old chronic/aggressive split

saqs.q: Describe the clinical characteristics of necrotizing periodontal diseases.
saqs.a: Ulcerated and necrotic papillary and marginal gingiva covered by a yellowish-white or grayish slough or pseudomembrane; blunting and cratering of the papillae; bleeding on provocation or spontaneous bleeding, pain and fetid breath; and possibly fever, malaise and lymphadenopathy.

list: Ulcerated and necrotic papillary and marginal gingiva, covered by a yellowish-white or grayish slough or pseudomembrane.
Blunting and cratering of the papillae.
Bleeding on provocation or spontaneous bleeding, pain, and fetid breath.
May be accompanied by fever, malaise and lymphadenopathy.

saqs.q: Compare necrotizing gingivitis, necrotizing periodontitis and necrotizing stomatitis.
saqs.a: NG has necrosis limited to the gingiva. NP shares the clinical features of NG but adds attachment and bone loss, and is often seen in HIV-positive individuals with low CD4 counts. NS is the most severe form, with soft tissue necrosis extending beyond the gingiva and bone denudation with bony sequestrum or osteitis.

head: Form
What defines it
rows: features of NG plus attachment and bone loss; often in HIV-positive patients with low CD4 counts
most severe — necrosis beyond the gingiva, bone denudation with sequestrum or osteitis

saqs.q: State the predisposing factors for necrotizing periodontal diseases and the response to treatment.
saqs.a: They are microbial, infectious conditions predisposed to by psychological stress, smoking, immunosuppression and malnutrition. They respond well to antimicrobial therapy combined with professional plaque and calculus removal.

list: Psychological stress
Smoking
Immunosuppression
Malnutrition

ans.text: All four lower host resistance. Being microbial infectious conditions, NPDs respond well to antimicrobial therapy combined with professional plaque and calculus removal.

saqs.q: Outline the periodontal manifestations of systemic diseases.
saqs.a: Several hematologic and genetic disorders lead to periodontitis, mainly through alterations in the immune response. Clinical manifestation appears at an early age with rapid CAL and early tooth loss. The major predisposing factor is the underlying disease and local factors are not clearly evident, so removal of local factors is inadequate to arrest the destruction.

list: Caused by several hematologic and genetic disorders.
Major effect is through alterations in the immune response.
Appears at an early age — rapid CAL and early tooth loss.
The underlying disease is the major predisposing factor; local factors are not clearly evident.
Removal of local factors is inadequate to arrest the periodontal destruction.

saqs.q: Describe Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome: diagnostic criteria, cause, and the timing of its signs.
saqs.a: Criteria are palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, loss of both the primary and permanent teeth, and autosomal-recessive inheritance from a cathepsin C gene mutation. Consanguinity of the parents is common. The primary cause is impaired neutrophil function, and the subgingival microbiota consists of opportunistic periodontal pathogens. Keratoderma usually appears with the first primary teeth at 5 to 6 months, sometimes as early as 1 month, and serum IgG against Aa is typically elevated.

list: Palmoplantar hyperkeratosis
Loss of the primary and the permanent teeth
Autosomal-recessive inheritance — mutation in the cathepsin C gene
Primary cause — impaired neutrophil function.
Subgingival microbiota — opportunistic periodontal pathogens; serum IgG against Aa typically elevated.
Consanguinity of the parents is a common finding; collect a full family history to identify undiagnosed siblings.

ans.text: Keratoderma usually appears simultaneously with eruption of the first primary teeth (5 to 6 months), but may appear as early as 1 month of age.

saqs.q: Define periodontitis and state the feature that distinguishes it from gingivitis.
saqs.a: Periodontitis is an inflammatory disease of the supporting tissues of the teeth caused by specific microorganisms or groups of specific microorganisms, resulting in progressive destruction of the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, with increased probing depth formation, recession, or both. The distinguishing clinical feature is clinical attachment loss, which appears as pocket formation and/or recession of the marginal gingiva.

list: An inflammatory disease of the supporting tissues of the teeth, caused by specific microorganisms or groups of specific microorganisms.
Resulting in progressive destruction of the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, with increased probing depth formation, recession, or both.

ans.text: The distinguishing clinical feature is CLINICAL ATTACHMENT LOSS — periodontal pocket formation and/or recession of the marginal gingiva.

saqs.q: Give the case definition of periodontitis, including the causes of attachment loss that must be excluded.
saqs.a: A patient is a periodontitis case if interdental CAL is detectable at two or more non-adjacent teeth, or if buccal or oral CAL of 3 mm or more with pocketing over 3 mm is detectable at two or more teeth. The CAL must not be ascribable to gingival recession of traumatic origin, subgingival caries, CAL on the distal of a second molar, an endodontic lesion draining through the sulcus, or a vertical root fracture.

ans.h: A patient is a periodontitis case if
steps: Interdental CAL is detectable at ≥ 2 non-adjacent teeth, OR
Buccal or oral CAL ≥ 3 mm with pocketing > 3 mm is detectable at ≥ 2 teeth.

ans.h: and the CAL cannot be ascribed to
list: gingival recession of traumatic origin
dental caries extending subgingivally
CAL on the distal aspect of a second molar
an endodontic lesion draining through the sulcus
a vertical root fracture

saqs.q: What does staging describe, and can a stage ever be lowered?
saqs.a: Staging describes the severity and complexity of each case, incorporating severity of disease and tooth loss due to periodontitis, and the management complexity and overall rehabilitation needs. It highlights the most severe areas of destruction and counts both missing teeth and teeth identified for extraction. If complexity factors are controlled after treatment the stage generally should not retrogress, because existing severity and previous complexity predict future progression; the only exception is significant bone gain after successful regenerative therapy.

list: Severity of the disease and tooth loss due to periodontitis.
Management complexity of the periodontal condition and overall oral rehabilitation needs.

ans.text: It highlights the patient's most severe areas of destruction, and counts missing teeth plus teeth identified for extraction as part of active therapy.

list: Generally no — existing severity (CAL and bone loss) and previous complexity factors predict future progression.
One exception — significant bone gain after successful regenerative therapy.

saqs.q: Tabulate the severity criteria for the four stages of periodontitis.
saqs.a: Interdental CAL at the worst site is 1–2 mm in Stage I, 3–4 mm in Stage II, and ≥5 mm in Stages III and IV. Radiographic bone loss is coronal third <15% in Stage I, coronal third 15–33% in Stage II, and extends to the mid-third of the root and beyond in Stages III and IV. Tooth loss due to periodontitis is none in Stages I and II, ≤4 teeth in Stage III, and ≥5 teeth in Stage IV.

ans.text: Tooth loss is the dividing line — CAL and bone loss alone cannot separate Stage III from Stage IV.

saqs.q: Tabulate the local complexity criteria of the four stages.
saqs.a: Stage I: maximum probing depth ≤4 mm with mostly horizontal bone loss. Stage II: maximum probing depth ≤5 mm with mostly horizontal bone loss. Stage III adds probing depth ≥6 mm, vertical bone loss ≥3 mm, furcation involvement Class II or III, and a moderate ridge defect. Stage IV adds the need for complex rehabilitation due to masticatory dysfunction, secondary occlusal trauma with mobility degree ≥2, severe ridge defect, bite collapse with drifting and flaring, and fewer than 20 remaining teeth.

head: Stage
Local complexity
rows: maximum probing depth ≤ 4 mm; mostly horizontal bone loss
maximum probing depth ≤ 5 mm; mostly horizontal bone loss

Stage III
in addition to stage II
probing depth ≥ 6 mm; vertical bone loss ≥ 3 mm; furcation Class II or III; moderate ridge defect

Stage IV
in addition to stage III
need for complex rehabilitation: masticatory dysfunction; secondary occlusal trauma (mobility ≥ 2); severe ridge defect; bite collapse, drifting, flaring; < 20 remaining teeth (10 opposing pairs)

saqs.q: How is the extent of periodontitis categorised?
saqs.a: By the percentage of teeth at the stage-defining severity level: localized is under 30% of teeth involved, generalized is 30% or more, and the third category is a molar-incisor pattern of involvement.

head: Extent
Criterion
rows: disease involvement follows the molar/incisor distribution

ans.text: Extent is a descriptor added to the stage, as in 'generalized Stage III'.

saqs.q: What does grading assess, and what evidence is used?
saqs.a: Grading analyses the rate of disease progression, the risk of further progression, the presence and control of risk factors, and general health modifiers. Direct evidence is longitudinal radiographic evaluation; indirect evidence is the percentage of bone loss relative to the patient's age. The grade is then modified by the presence of risk factors.

list: Analysis of the rate of disease progression.
Assessment of the risk for further progression.
Presence and control of risk factors.
General health modifiers.
Direct — longitudinal radiographic evaluation.
Indirect — percentage of bone loss with respect to the patient's age.

saqs.q: Tabulate the primary criteria and grade modifiers for grades A, B and C.
saqs.a: Direct evidence: no loss over 5 years is A, under 2 mm is B, 2 mm or more is C. Percentage bone loss over age: under 0.25 is A, 0.25 to 1.0 is B, over 1.0 is C. Case phenotype: heavy deposits with low destruction is A, destruction commensurate with deposits is B, destruction exceeding expectation is C. Smoking: non-smoker is A, under 10 cigarettes a day is B, 10 or more is C. Diabetes: normoglycemic is A, HbA1c under 7.0% in a diabetic is B, 7.0% or more is C.

head: Criterion
Grade A — slow
Grade B — moderate
Grade C — rapid
rows: destruction exceeds expectation; molar/incisor pattern; poor response to standard therapy

saqs.q: List the five groups of 'other conditions affecting the periodontium'.
saqs.a: Systemic diseases or conditions affecting the periodontal supporting tissues; periodontal abscesses and endodontic-periodontal lesions; mucogingival deformities and conditions; traumatic occlusal forces; and tooth and prosthesis related factors.

list: a. Systemic diseases or conditions affecting the periodontal supporting tissues
b. Periodontal abscesses and endodontic–periodontal lesions
c. Mucogingival deformities and conditions
d. Traumatic occlusal forces
e. Tooth and prosthesis related factors

saqs.q: Classify the systemic diseases and conditions affecting the periodontal supporting structures.
saqs.a: They have a negative impact on the attachment apparatus independent of biofilm-induced inflammation. Neoplasms: oral squamous cell carcinoma, odontogenic tumors, other primary neoplasms and secondary metastatic neoplasms. Other disorders: Langerhans cell histiocytosis, giant cell granulomas, hyperparathyroidism and systemic sclerosis.

head: Group
Members
rows: oral squamous cell carcinoma · odontogenic tumors · other primary neoplasms · secondary metastatic neoplasms
Langerhans cell histiocytosis · giant cell granulomas · hyperparathyroidism · systemic sclerosis

ans.text: They affect the periodontal tissues independent of biofilm-induced inflammation.

saqs.q: Define a periodontal abscess and give its aetiological classification.
saqs.a: A localized acute and purulent infection within the gingival wall of the periodontal pocket. Tissue destruction is rapid with a risk of systemic dissemination, so it requires immediate management. It is classified by aetiology into pre-existing deep periodontal pockets, foreign body reactions, and overgrowth of opportunistic bacteria.

list: A localized acute and purulent infection within the gingival wall of the periodontal pocket.
Tissue destruction is rapid, with risk of systemic dissemination — requires immediate management.

saqs.q: Define an endodontic–periodontal lesion and list its aetiological factors and its signs and symptoms.
saqs.a: A pathological communication between the pulpal and periodontal tissues. Aetiology is endodontic and/or periodontal infections, and trauma and/or iatrogenic factors such as root fracture or cracking, root perforation, external root resorption or pulp necrosis. Signs include deep pockets reaching the root apex, altered response to pulp vitality tests, spontaneous pain and pain on percussion, a sinus tract, gingival inflammation and suppuration, tooth mobility, and bone loss in the periapical or furcation region.

list: Endodontic and/or periodontal infections.
Trauma and/or iatrogenic factors — root fracture or cracking, root perforation, external root resorption, pulp necrosis.
Deep periodontal pockets reaching to the root apex
Altered response to pulp vitality tests
Spontaneous pain, pain on percussion, presence of a sinus tract
Gingival inflammation, suppuration
Tooth mobility, and bone loss in the periapical or furcation region

saqs.q: List the mucogingival deformities and conditions around teeth.
saqs.a: Gingival/soft tissue recession on facial or lingual surfaces and interproximally; lack of keratinized gingiva; decreased vestibular depth; aberrant frenum or muscle position; gingival excess as pseudo-pocket, inconsistent gingival margin, excessive gingival display or gingival enlargement; and abnormal colour.

list: 1. Gingival/soft tissue recession — a. facial or lingual surfaces; b. interproximal (papillary)
2. Lack of keratinized gingiva
3. Decreased vestibular depth
4. Aberrant frenum / muscle position
5. Gingival excess — a. pseudo-pocket; b. inconsistent gingival margin; c. excessive gingival display; d. gingival enlargement
6. Abnormal color

saqs.q: Define gingival recession and give the Cairo classification.
saqs.a: An apical shift in the position of the gingival margin with exposure of the root surface, classified on interdental CAL. RT1 has only buccal attachment loss with no interproximal loss; RT2 has interproximal loss less than or equal to the buccal loss; RT3 has interproximal loss higher than the buccal loss.

ans.text: Gingival recession is an apical shift in the position of the gingival margin with exposure of the root surface.

saqs.q: Define traumatic occlusal force, and list the tooth and prosthesis related factors that predispose to periodontal disease.
saqs.a: A traumatic occlusal force is an occlusal force that exceeds the reparative capacity of the periodontal attachment apparatus and results in occlusal trauma; multiple clinical and radiographic indicators assist its diagnosis. Localized tooth related factors are cervical enamel projections and enamel pearls, developmental grooves, tooth and root fractures, and root resorption. Localized prosthesis related factors are fixed dental restorations and prostheses, dental materials, and removable dental prostheses.

ans.text: A traumatic occlusal force exceeds the reparative capacity of the periodontal attachment apparatus and results in occlusal trauma; multiple clinical and radiographic indicators assist the diagnosis.

saqs.q: List the peri-implant diseases and conditions and distinguish the first three.
saqs.a: Peri-implant health, peri-implant mucositis, peri-implantitis, and peri-implant soft and hard tissue deficiencies. Health shows absence of visual signs of inflammation and lack of BOP. Mucositis shows visual signs of inflammation and/or BOP but without loss of supportive or marginal bone. Peri-implantitis shows inflammation and/or BOP accompanied by progressive loss of supportive bone.
